name: Wayuu
confidence_why: Álvarez 2021, Mosonyi & Jackson 1994-96 and the Mansens' own descriptions (Mansen 1967; Mansen & Mansen 1976, 1984) all give the same rule, stress on a heavy first syllable (long vowel, diphthong or closed) and otherwise on the second, with an initial vowel-glottal-stop-vowel sequence counting as one syllable, and the few minimal pairs on which Mansen 1967 calls stress phonemic (eittáwaa 'put' vs éittawaa 'return') are exactly the accent-marked exceptions the later works list, so the sources converge on a weight-sensitive system with a small lexical residue.

catalog_quote: 1.6. En wayuunaiki es crucial la noción de PESO SILÁBICO. Una sílaba liviana (L) contiene una sola vocal corta V. Una sílaba pesada (P) contiene una vocal larga V1V1, un diptongo V1V2, o una vocal seguida de una consonante que cierra la sílaba VC. Para esta distinción es indiferente si la sílaba tiene o no una consonante inicial. 1.7. Las reglas para determinar la SÍLABA TÓNICA en una palabra son: a. Si la primera sílaba es liviana, es tónica la segunda sílaba: a cha ja waa ... ta tü na ... e kaa sü ... n no jo lee chi ... b. Si la primera sílaba es pesada, es tónica esa misma primera sílaba: aa sha ja waa ... ei ma la waa ... tou sa jüin ... at sha ... tün taa ... c. Si al inicio de palabra hay una secuencia (C)V’ (donde V es una vocal corta), la sílaba inicial es extramétrica, es decir, no se cuenta. Cuando esto sucede, se cuenta la segunda sílaba como primera: o ’u nu su (Ø 1 2 3) ..…

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is treated as phonemic (contrastive), shown by minimal pairs such as tawará 'my hair' vs. tawára 'my brother' and eittáwaa 'to put' vs. éittawaa 'to return'; its main cue is high pitch rather than intensity, and pitch is predictable from stress plus syllable type. No placement rule is given in this paper; the headnote (p. 49) notes that a Spanish loan (zanahoria > sanáooria) has its stress 'shifted forward' and that 'the phonemic syllable is a unit of potential stress placement' (p. 57).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described; the paper says that 'words with apparent multiple stress' have only one high-pitched syllable (p. 56).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions; the paper gives only contrastive pairs and no rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Mansen & Mansen 1976 (p. 255) state that their data come from the central Colombian Guajira Peninsula and that the main consultant, Guillermo Estrada Uriana, speaks the 'Arribero' dialect of the upper peninsula; Guajiro is described there as having several mutually intelligible dialects. Mansen 1967 and Mansen & Mansen 1984 are by the same authors and presumably describe the same Colombian variety. The Rosetta/Mosonyi 2000 file already held by the project (not in the target list) describes Venezuelan Wayuunaiki and gives IPA transcriptions with stress marks but no rule.

new_statements.quote: 2.1 Acento. Por lo general, en el guajiro el patrón del acento es predecible. En palabras de dos o más sílabas, el acento fuerte se dará en una de las siguientes: (1) la primera sílaba; (2) la segunda sílaba; o (3) alguna otra sílaba. 2.1.1 En la primera sílaba. Las palabras en las cuales el acento recae en la primera sílaba comienzan con una vocal geminada (VV), con una consonante y vocal geminada (CVV), o con una sílaba cerrada (VC o CVC). [...] 2.1.2 En la segunda sílaba. En el guajiro la mayoría de las palabras tiene acento fuerte en la segunda sílaba. A menos que el acento aparezca en la primera sílaba (como se mencionó anteriormente), y a menos que se señale con una tilde ( ´ ), el acento cae en la segunda sílaba.
new_statements.translation: 2.1 Stress. In general, in Guajiro the stress pattern is predictable. In words of two or more syllables, the main stress falls on one of the following: (1) the first syllable; (2) the second syllable; or (3) some other syllable. 2.1.1 On the first syllable. Words in which the stress falls on the first syllable begin with a geminate vowel (VV), with a consonant plus geminate vowel (CVV), or with a closed syllable (VC or CVC). [...] 2.1.2 On the second syllable. In Guajiro most words have main stress on the second syllable. Unless the stress appears on the first syllable (as mentioned above), and unless it is marked with an acute accent, the stress falls on the second syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog rule is empty; this is the fullest statement found: a predictable weight-sensitive rule (heavy initial syllable -> initial stress, else second syllable) with lexically marked exceptions. Compatible with Mansen 1967's contrastive pairs, which appear here as the marked exceptions.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the first syllable when that syllable is heavy (long/geminate vowel or closed by a consonant); otherwise it falls on the second syllable, which is the majority pattern. A word-initial V'V sequence (vowel-glottal stop-vowel) counts as a single vowel/syllable for this rule (p. 5 and the note on p. 9), so stress lands on the following syllable (a'atapajaa [aʔa'tapaha:] 'to wait', o'unaa [oʔu'na:] 'to go'). Words that do not fit are written with an acute accent on the stressed syllable (ayatáwaa 'to work', nójotsü 'there is none', eittáwaa 'to put, to bet').
new_statements.exceptions: Sec. 2.1.3: words that do not follow the pattern carry a written accent; 'Hay algunos casos en los cuales el acento no sigue un patrón y ocasiona un cambio en el significado' (there are some cases where stress does not follow a pattern and changes meaning): ayalajaa [a'yařaha:] 'to buy' vs. ayalájaa [aya'řaha:] 'to cry'; eittawaa ['eittawa:] 'to return' vs. eittáwaa [eit'tawa:] 'to put, to bet'.

new_statements.quote: There is one short or geminate vowel per syllable. Stress generally falls on the second syllable (or the third syllable following a vowel-glottal stop-vowel sequence) unless the first syllable is closed or has a geminate vowel, in which case stress falls on the first. No special stress mark is written when stress falls in either of those positions. An acute accent is written to indicate that stress falls elsewhere.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default stress on the second syllable (third when the word begins with a V'V sequence); if the first syllable is heavy (closed or with a geminate/long vowel) stress falls on the first syllable; other placements are lexical and written with an acute accent. The paper also notes at the sentence level that in binary juxtaposed sentences 'sentence stress occurs but once, and in the first clause' (p. 184).
new_statements.exceptions: Words whose stress falls elsewhere than the two default positions are marked with an acute accent (no examples given in the footnote; it refers to Mansen 1967 for the full phonemic statement).

The Rosetta/Mosonyi 2000 file already held by the project (not in the target list) describes Venezuelan Wayuunaiki and gives IPA transcriptions with stress marks but no rule.

readall_conflicts: No real disagreement. Mansen 1967 (and the Waterhouse volume that contains it) presents stress as phonemic/contrastive with minimal pairs and gives no placement rule, while Mansen & Mansen 1976 (fn. 2, pp. 255-256) and Mansen & Mansen 1984 (ch. 1, sec. 2.1, pp. 8-9) state a predictable weight-sensitive rule (heavy first syllable, i.e. closed or long-vowelled, takes stress; otherwise the second syllable, or the third after an initial V'V) with lexically marked exceptions. The 1967 minimal pairs (eittáwaa 'put' vs. éittawaa 'return') are exactly the accent-marked exceptions of the later works, so the sources are consistent: a default weight-sensitive rule with a residue of lexical contrasts.
